content: I'm reviewing a document called "The Thesis" by David Jaz Myers, Matteo Capucci, Jason Brown with contributions from Diptarko Roy, Eigil Fjeldgren Rischel, Grigory Neustroev, Mirco Giacobbe. This describes a double categorical approach to cyberphysical systems. I don't have the power (or right) to share this document, but David Jaz and also the agency funding him have said it's fine for me to discuss it as I read it. So I'll do that here.

The introduction has been rewritten since I last looked at it, so I'll start there. I apologize for the sketchy nature of my comments.

Their first approach to systems is to consider a functor

Behaviors→Sh(Clocks) \text{Behaviors} \to \text{Sh}(\text{Clocks}) Behaviors→Sh(Clocks)

In cases where behaviors might not extend forever (such as transition systems that can halt, or ODEs which might blow up in finite time), it is better to consider partial orders or whole categories of clocks, rather than just the monoid of endomorphisms of a single ‘global’ clock. In general, we find that behaviors assemble into sheaves on categories of clocks.

Here they are following Schultz, Spivak and Vasilakopoulou's Dynamical systems and sheaves.

Next they consider three ways of describing systems, with functors from the first to the second and from the second to the third. I think their example makes the basic idea clear, at least to me:

They promise to formalize this very generally.

The first approach they call "ontological", a scary word - but it simply means we're saying what there is in the system, e.g. a resistor, inductor, capacitor and current source (voltage source?) connected by wires. They give examples of different kinds of ontological models - electric circuit diagrams are just one, of course. For each kind, we also get to define homomorphisms between such models.

They then turn to "open" ontological models, and how we can use operads to describe ways of gluing together such open models. The relevant algebras of these operads are not mere structured collections of sets (as typical of operad algebras) but rather structured collections of categories, since we not only have a set of open models with some particular choice of boundary data, but a category of them.
(All this is very familiar to me, luckily, because I happen to have been thinking about it for a long time. Thus, I won't explain it as well as I should!)

They conclude this section with a taste of the practical applications of these ideas: "assume-guarantee reasoning" where if you assume something about the behavior of a bunch of open systems being composed - that is, composed via some operation in some operad - you can guarantee something about the behavior of the composite system.

This is the kind of reasoning we often use when building complicated machines out of parts. It deserves to be formalized:

  • Matteo Capucci, David Jaz Myers, Compositionality of Lyapunov functions via assume-guarantee reasoning.

Then comes a draft outline of a vision of "Mathematical modeling in the 21st century".

The first point is that we should "separate the conceptual model (the presentation or definition of the model) from the computation of the model (solving it, checking it, running it, etc.)". The work of @Nathaniel Osgood, @Evan Patterson, and many others takes this approach, calling it declarative modeling - I guess as opposed to imperative or procedural modeling.

In this approach, a model is fundamentally a mathematical object, not a piece of code saying how to compute something. (A great example is the electric circuit diagram I showed earlier.)

Declarative modelling is not quite declarative programming. Declarative programming describes a program; declarative modelling describes a model.

However, there are many different languages for declarative modeling: not only electric circuit diagrams, but Petri nets, stock and flow models, chemical reaction networks, and many many more. Many of these languages come in large families containing many variants. To take a simple example, as soon as we create a language for describing circuits with resistors, capacitors, inductors, current sources and voltage sources, someone is going to want to add transistors. Or memristors, etcetera. There are also dozens of different widely used kinds of Petri nets.

Thus, we need a language for specifying declarative modeling languages!

This language too should be declarative, so we need to understand declarative meta-modeling.

They write:

To be able to declare meta-models, we need a meta-meta-model: a model of meta-models.

  1. A unified framework for declaring meta-models, models within them, translations between them, and calling out to specially written analysis tools on a meta-model basis.
  2. Design space is enormous; we should be constrained by a clean mathematical semantics.
  3. Should we also have declarative meta-meta-models? Some day we will surely find ourselves wanting this, but not our focus right now.

Whew. So, we do not climb up this infinite ladder, at least not today.

Then comes an outline of what's to come:

We will cover:

A broad variety of categories of models, including various kinds of dynamical systems (discrete-time (Chapter 2.2), continuous-time, deterministic, stochastic, differential), systems dynamics models, relational databases (Chapter 2.3), hybrid models like coloured Petri nets (Chapter 2.4).

Specifications of model behaviours (Section 3.1.2.7). Categorical approach to the logic (Chapter 3.2)

Translations between these as functors (Section 2.2.3, Section 2.3.10).

Representability of behaviour of models by morphisms; representability of safety certificates (Lyapunov functions) by morphisms (Section 3.1.3.2, Section 2.2.4.3).

Behaviour functors land in time-varying sets (sheaves on clocks) (Section 3.1.3)

The internal logic of sheaves on clocks is a temporal modal logic (Section 3.2.1)

Properties of behaviours of systems specified in these modal logics may be checked (to a degree of certainty) by exhibiting Lyapunov or control-barrier functions (Section 3.2.2, Chapter 3.3).

Neural-Lyapunov approach to system certification (Section 3.3.6).

Compositionality of models via 2-algebraic structure on categories of models (Chapter 4.3).

A particular focus on operadic composition: declarative modularity (Chapter 4.2).

The coupling law / interaction pattern is itself declared; 2-algebraic operations are objects themselves (just as 1-algebraic operations (terms) are themselves elements).

These include wiring diagrams, string diagrams, etc. (Section 4.3.3, Section 4.4.2)

Compositionality of certified systems using assume-guarantee reasoning. This has not made it into the current draft strongly, but the main idea is that fibrations of 2-algebras give a basic setting for compositional certification. This also includes the Hoare logic approach to verification with pre- and post- conditions; it depends on the particular 2-algebraic theory and the particular 2-algebras involved (Chapter 4.6).

Compositionality of translations: functors preserve compositional structure (Chapter 4.4).

Compositionality of behaviour functors (Chapter 4.5). This is via a general representability theorem that applies at the level of 2-algebra generally, and so works with any 2-algebra of modularity (Expert-Section 4.5.4).

Willems' behavioural control theory (variable sharing) as universal (meta-)meta-model. Specfically, via nerves from categories (or more generally 2-algebras, though this is not covered in the thesis right now) of clocks valued in discrete opfibration classifiers for 2-algebraic structures, giving us compositionality theorems landing in “temporal” (pre)sheaf toposes (Section 4.3.3, Expert-Section 4.5.4).

Barrelling onwards... Chapter 2.1 is about "categories of systems". It begins with many examples of "systems" and "models", to lay out the challenge of covering all these examples in a unified framework.

They talk a lot about something I've never talked about enough: using morphisms between systems for a wide variety of purposes:

Maps have not gone unnoticed in mathematical modelling; in fact, they show up all over the place under various names like “simulation”, “coarse-graining”, “invariant subset”, “motif”, “Lyapunov function”, “control barrier function”, “labeling”, “colouring”, and so on.

I've written about "coarse-graining" (mapping a complicated model down to a cruder one) and also the inclusion of a simple model in a more complicated one: these are at least morally like epis and monos. But I think of David Spivak and others as promoting other uses.

For example, in the category of discrete-time deterministic dynamical systems, the terminal object is the dynamical system with one state, which of course never changes with time. A morphism from this to another dynamical system is the same as a fixed point in that other system.

We can use similar tricks to capture (or more precisely, 'represent') orbits of a specific period.

There is another important discrete-time dynamical system, the 'clock', which has one state per integer, and one step of time evolution maps the nth state to the (n+1)st state. A map from this discrete-time dynamical system to any other is a run of that other system.

Note all three examples above are about cyclic groups viewed as dynamical systems, with the 1-element cyclic group and infinite cyclic group playing somewhat special roles, as picking out 'fixed points' and 'runs'.

Chapter 2 contains many more examples of systems, including

  • Moore machines,
  • partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs),
  • ordinary differential equations

and I won't go into them all, but instead note this:

In total, we see that Moore machines, POMDPs, and ODEs can be put in the same form: we have a span of bundles.

The easiest example is perhaps a Moore machine:

  1. At left in our span of bundles we have the bundle of "changes of state". For a Moore machine this is just the bundle π1 ⁣:S×S→S\pi_1 \colon S \times S \to Sπ1​:S×S→S where SSS is a set of 'states'. Elements of S×SS \times SS×S are pairs consisting of the state now and the next state. This is like a discrete version of a tangent bundle, and this analogy is important for understanding what's going on.
  2. In the middle of our span of bundles is the bundle of state-action pairs π1 ⁣:S×A→S\pi_1 \colon S \times A \to Sπ1​:S×A→S where AAA is a set of 'actions'. This bundle maps to the bundle in 1 because a Moore machine has a map u ⁣:S×A→Su \colon S \times A \to Su:S×A→S saying how a state now and an action determines the next state. So, the left leg of our span is the real meat of the Moore machine.
  3. At the right of our span of bundles is the bundle of observation-action pairs π1 ⁣:O×A→O\pi_1 \colon O \times A \to Oπ1​:O×A→O where OOO is a set of observations. The bundle in 1 maps to this one because a Moore machine also has a map v ⁣:S→Ov \colon S \to Ov:S→O saying how a state now determines an 'observation': we observe something about the state and get an element of OOO.

I'm not quite in love with this spanish approach to Moore machines, but it can be generalized to handle ODE - and I certainly love how when we do this, the tangent bundle TS→ST S \to STS→S of a manifold of states replaces the bundle π1 ⁣:S×S→S\pi_1 \colon S \times S \to Sπ1​:S×S→S associated to a set of states. I think I'm more in love with bundles 1 and 2 in the above list than bundle 3.

They generalize the heck out of this idea:

We can therefore give a definition of these generalised Moore machines if we have a notion of bundle and a functorial choice of “tangent bundles”, or bundles of possible changes.

They want to simultaneously generalize the concept of the tangent bundle TS→STS \to STS→S of a manifold SSS and the bundle π1 ⁣:S×S→S\pi_1 \colon S \times S \to Sπ1​:S×S→S where SSS is a mere set. They do this using a concept they call a 'tangency':

A tangency consists of a cartesian fibration π:E→B\pi :E\to Bπ:E→B together with a section, i.e. a functor T:B→ET:B\to ET:B→E such that π∘T=idB\pi \circ T=\text{id}_Bπ∘T=idB​.

This reminds me of the microcosm principle, since BBB and EEE here is a category, and the fibration π ⁣:E→B\pi \colon E \to Bπ:E→B is like a categorified bundle over BBB - but we are using it to define a kind of tangent bundle TSTSTS for any object S∈BS \in BS∈B. For any 'base space' S∈BS \in BS∈B we get a 'tangent bundle' TS∈ETS \in ETS∈E, and the base space of this tangent bundle is π(TS)=S\pi(TS) = Sπ(TS)=S.

But there's a lot around this passage that I don't understand yet, unlike previous sections where I sort of knew the stuff. So, I will need to take a break soon.

Instead of just describing generalized Moore machines, they want machines with 'interfaces', presumably since the goal is to formalize open systems.

We now have the ingredients ready. It's time to describe the recipe for arranging the data of a tangency into a category of Moore machines. However, it will still be useful to separate the category of interfaces from the category of systems. Therefore, unlike the previous recipes we've seen (Definition 2.2.2.6 and Theorem 2.2.3.6), this recipe will not produce a single category of systems but rather a displayed category of systems, displayed over the category of interfaces.

Fear not: a displayed category is defined to simply be a functor! But it's a functor with attitude. :laughing: (See the nLab article [[concept with attitude]] if you don't know what I mean.)

A displayed category is a functor ∂ ⁣:D→I \partial \colon D \to I∂:D→I where for each object i∈Ii \in Ii∈I, called an interface, there's a category over it, namely the fiber of ∂\partial∂ over iii.

So, it's like a fibration minus all the fancy stuff.

(BTW, the reason it's worth emphasising it's conceptually different than a functor is that once you equip your categories with algebraic structure, your display maps start being specifically strict functors, so they are somewhat fancier. In general, you'd like to also have them be isofibrations, meaning isomorphic interfaces support isomorphic categories of systems with such interface.)
Yay I'm glad you're doing an open review :D so much more valuable

Okay, I'm back to trying to understand open dynamical systems from the perspective of this paper. I will try to fit two examples I understand into this perspective.

  1. A Moore machine is a set SSS of states, a set OOO of observations, a set AAA of actions, a map
    u ⁣:S×A→Su \colon S \times A \to Su:S×A→S
    which gives a new state as a function of an old state and an action, and a map
    v ⁣:S→O v \colon S \to Ov:S→O
    saying what you'll observe as a function of the state. This is the material discussed right above Lemma 2.2.4.1.2.

  2. A parametrized ordinary differential equation is a manifold SSS of states, a manifold OOO of observations, a manifold AAA of parameters, a smooth map uuu that sends any state s∈Ss \in Ss∈S and any parameter a∈Aa \in Aa∈A to a tangent vector u(s,a)∈TsSu(s,a) \in T_s Su(s,a)∈Ts​S, and a map
    v ⁣:S→O v \colon S \to Ov:S→O
    saying what you're observe as a function of the state. This is secretly what is being discussed in Example 2.2.4.1.6.

I want to understand how examples 1 and 2 are both shoehorned into the same formalism.

The v ⁣:S→Ov \colon S \to Ov:S→O part works the same in both cases, but
u ⁣:A×S→Su \colon A \times S \to Su:A×S→S
in example 1 looks different from what's going on in example 2. In fact we need to redescribe both examples in somewhat different ways to make them look the same.

For example 1, we note that u ⁣:A×S→Su \colon A \times S \to Su:A×S→S can be used to define a map of 'bundles' (bundles of mere sets) from the bundle
π1 ⁣:S×A→S\pi_1 \colon S \times A \to Sπ1​:S×A→S
(which picks out the state from a state-action pair) to the bundle
π1 ⁣:S×S→S \pi_1 \colon S \times S \to Sπ1​:S×S→S
(which picks out the old state from an old state - new state pair). The second bundle is analogous to a tangent bundle, since an "old state - new state pair" is a lot like a "position - velocity" pair.

So, in our quest for unification, we want to also phrase example 2 as a map of bundles (but now bundles of manifolds). This will be a map from the bundle
π1 ⁣:S×A→S\pi_1 \colon S \times A \to Sπ1​:S×A→S
(which picks out the state from a state-parameter pair) to the bundle
π ⁣:TS→S \pi \colon TS \to Sπ:TS→S
given by the usual projection from the tangent bundle TSTSTS to SSS (which picks out the state from a "state-velocity pair").

As in example 1, this map of bundles is the identity on the base SSS. On the total space it's a map u ⁣:S×A→TSu \colon S \times A \to TSu:S×A→TS that sends any state s∈Ss \in Ss∈S and any parameter a∈Aa \in Aa∈A to a tangent vector u(s,a)∈TsSu(s,a) \in T_s Su(s,a)∈Ts​S. The fact that u(s,a)u(s,a)u(s,a) lies in TsST_sSTs​S is enforced by the fact that we have a map of bundles.

So here the "map of bundles" nonsense is actually pulling its weight.

But now that we're in the mood for having everything be a map of bundles, we want to phrase our humble map from states to observations
v ⁣:S→O v \colon S \to Ov:S→O
as again a map of bundles! Don't ask why: we just do.

So, we think of it as a map from our bundle
π1 ⁣:S×A→A\pi_1 \colon S \times A \to Aπ1​:S×A→A
to the bundle
π1 ⁣:O×A→A \pi_1 \colon O \times A \to Aπ1​:O×A→A
This bundle map is made up of identity morphisms except for v ⁣:S→Ov \colon S \to Ov:S→O.

So we did it! We have expressed both kinds of dynamical systems with observations as spans of bundles. :tada:

For example 1, this span looks like this:

After doing example 1, the thesis says

This is a span of bundles. Not every such span encodes a Moore machine, but we can characterize those that do.

Presumably this characterization, when phrased abstractly enough, also handles example 2.
Yes. The thesis does this using concepts like 'tangency', 'displayed category', etc.

I found the above formalism hard to absorb not so much because a span of bundles is complicated, but because it seems concocted rather arbitrarily and the two legs of the span play very different roles. In both example I discussed, the left leg says "how a state and an action determine the future" while the right leg says "how a state determines an observation", with the action basically going along for the ride.

Maybe if I had a good understanding of lenses this would all make more sense. (The thesis mentions them here.)

Okay, that's enough for this pass through Chapter 2.2: Categories of dynamical systems. I didn't completely explain the formalism for dynamical systems, nor did I did I cover all the examples in the thesis: I only went through two examples and sketched how they can be seen as analogous and thus fit into a common formalism.

Next:

Chapter 2.3: Categories of schematic systems

In this chapter we present another modelling paradigm — models as databases. Whereas the salient feature of a dynamical system is how it evolves, i.e. its dynamics, the salient feature of models presented in the database-paradigm is how they are structured — i.e. how they are decomposed into collections of elements which admit structural relations to each other. Just as in Chapter 2.2, it will be convenient to have a general term to express the attitude of this paradigm, without necessarily prescribing a formalism. The term we shall use is schematic system, both as an allusion to schemas in the sense of database theory and to the graphical representations that models of such theories necessarily admit. To that last point, many of the examples of categories of systems with a “graphical flavour” are schematic, including:

  1. directed graphs
  2. circuit digrams
  3. Petri nets
  4. stock–flow diagrams
  5. causal loop diagrams
  6. labelled/coloured/decorated versions of the above

Many of these are very familiar to me, so I expect I'll mainly focus on how all these examples get put into a common formalism.

In both example I discussed, the left leg says "how a state and an action determine the future" while the right leg says "how a state determines an observation", with the action basically going along for the ride.

I wonder if the same "span of bundles" approach could be used to describe a situation where we have a map that says "how a state together with an action determines an observation".

The idea is that our set of "actions" now correspond to different ways to obtain an observation. This situation is common in medical imaging, where for any given state of the thing we wish to observe, there are many different ways we can choose to act so as to obtain an observation.

Hi! Long time no see! What you're asking for seems reasonable, and it reminds me more of a "Mealy machine" than a "Moore machine".

A Moore machine, just to remind myself, has a map

u ⁣:S×A→Su \colon S \times A \to Su:S×A→S

which gives a new state as a function of an old state and an action, and a map

v ⁣:S→Ov \colon S \to Ov:S→O

A Mealy machine instead has a single map

u ⁣:S×A→S×O u \colon S \times A \to S \times Ou:S×A→S×O

which gives a new state and an observation as a function of an old state and an action. So, the observation can depend on the action.
I believe, and hope, that the formalism they described easily generalizes to Mealy machines, just by replacing the map v×Av \times Av×A in this diagram by uuu:

I think I said this in my description. I also explained how the parametrized continuous time, continuous space system with observable variables of states fit into the same general formalism. That's cool.

Put this way, it sounds pretty cool. The problem was that I'm vastly more used to spans (and cospans) where the two legs play symmetrical roles: I've written plenty of papers about those. But I may be getting over this. I think it would have helped me a lot if the thesis had said "we're going to describe dynamical systems using a spans of bundles where the left leg says how states and parameters affect future states, while the right leg says how states and parameters affect what we observe now".

It was new for me too, but then again there was a lot that was new for me while learning about this so at the time I figured it must just be me being new to CT :)
It took a bit to remember and find but I did manage to locate where David discusses it, I believe it's here from around 41m54s onwards to around the 51m mark where he talks about some interesting properties of these Spans with vertical left leg and cartesian right leg (such as any of these squares can be factorized into them) and how they arrive at them.

Thanks! Yes, when you're first learning a subject one is more willing to accept any crazy stuff that people throw at you. Later, when you think you know something, you can react in a more fussy way when encountering something weird and new. I'll check out that part of the video.

In both example I discussed, the left leg says "how a state and an action determine the future" while the right leg says "how a state determines an observation", with the action basically going along for the ride.

Part of the issue here is that the "morphism direction" here (or in lenses) doesn't coincide with the flow of information. It's best to think of left and right here as inside and outside.

The dynamics loop

  • Starts at the bottom left with an internal state.
  • This determines (or is constrained by) an observable state at the boundary.
  • ...
  • The environment responds by returning an action at the top right.
  • The right-hand (pullback) square copies this action into over the internal state.
  • Finally, the action and state together determine the next state (discrete) or flow (cts)

So information flows out, then back in, then loops to determine the dynamic. It's worth noting that the lens/span of bundles doesn't control the environmental response. That just says a component can participate in many different dynamics, depending on the behavior of it's neighbors. To fully specify a single dynamical trajectory, we have to build a closed system, which corresponds equivalently to

  • a map (lens) into the "unit" bundle y:1→1y: 1 \to 1y:1→1.
  • a section of the bundle that is the domain of the map
  • a function from observable state to compatible actions

This is not too far from objective linear algebra, but here the action of the "matrix" is going right-to-left. We think of actions as a vector indexed by observations. Then we pull back to copy/delete some of the factors. I'm not sure how to interpret the left-hand square in these terms, though

I wonder how much the book says of this, but my understanding is that there are 2 separate things going on here. The first is the construction of the fibrewise opposite of a fibred category as a category of spans whose legs are cartesian and vertical. This construction comes up a lot in lens world but has nothing specifically to do with them, and it "explains" why spans are involved at all

The second thing is what's special about the object (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) on the left, which I have no idea how to talk about in a correspondingly abstract way. Over at Glaive we recently figured out what we're pretty sure is the right way to think about this (to be precise, by "this" I mean David Jaz's encoding of state machines as lenses). The fact about the object (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) that you actually should need to make things work is that it is a comonoid of the composition product of polynomial functors. It is a meme fact that such comonoids correspond 1-1 to small categories (but their homomorphisms do not correspond to functors), and (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) specifically is an indiscrete category, ie. one with exactly 1 morphism between each pair of objects. This fact appears in the Poly book. The intuitive idea is that a state change is nothing but naming a new state and throwing away the old one.

However, many of the examples from the book I believe form categories that don't come with something that looks exactly like a composition product, so I'm curious if the true form can be figured out from what they do. I vaguely suspect that it might involve some differential geometry word like "connection" or something

The formalism of tangencies is much more flexible than that. It seems to me that it's comonoids being a special instance of this construction rather than their 'true form'.
We have a bias towards being able to actually do the transition, even when it's non-deterministic, or infinitesimal, when in practice it is enough to be able to say what it means for a trajectory to conform to a given transition at every state. Separating these two moments is one of the good ideas of DOTS.

Jules Hedges said:

The second thing is what's special about the object (S,S)(S, S)(S,S) on the left, which I have no idea how to talk about in a correspondingly abstract way.

These are picked by the section TTT of the fibration. This section is used by the construction of the displayed category of Moore machines to fix what it means to be a 'stateful boundary'. Essentially, Moore machines are defined by the slice T/LensT/\bf LensT/Lens so that they are lenses with a stateful boundary on the left. Specifically, TTT chooses for every SSS state space a dependent type (though we work semantically) s:S⊢TsSs:S \vdash T_s Ss:S⊢Ts​S that gives, at every state, the menu of options to change the state. The dynamics of the Moore machine will produce a change of state from this menu then.
Note also a morphism (a chart) is forced to be, on the left boundary, something of the form (Tff){Tf \choose f}(fTf​), ie to be determined by a map on state space alone. These are then what determine that a trajectory will be something that at every moment changes in the same way as the Moore machine prescribes.

Back to business: I should have noted Lemma 2.2.4.12, which says that a Moore machine is a kind of lens. There's a kind of lens that's a pair of morphisms u:S′×A→S,v:S→Ou:S' \times A \to S, v: S \to Ou:S′×A→S,v:S→O , and if we take S′=SS' = SS′=S this is just a Moore machine as described here.

Skipping over a wealth of further material in Section 2.2, now let me talk about Section 2.3: Categories of schematic systems. It begins:

In this chapter we present another modelling paradigm — models as databases. Whereas the salient feature of a dynamical system is how it evolves, i.e. its dynamics, the salient feature of models presented in the database-paradigm is how they are structured — i.e. how they are decomposed into collections of elements which admit structural relations to each other. Just as in Chapter 2.2 [which discussed dynamical systems], it will be convenient to have a general term to express the attitude of this paradigm, without necessarily prescribing a formalism. The term we shall use is schematic system, both as an allusion to schemas in the sense of database theory and to the graphical representations that models of such theories necessarily admit. To that last point, many of the examples of categories of systems with a “graphical flavour” are schematic, including:

  1. directed graphs
  2. circuit digrams
  3. Petri nets
  4. stock–flow diagrams
  5. causal loop diagrams
  6. labelled/coloured/decorated versions of the above

In this chapter we will explore the various ways in which schematic systems assemble into categories via a formalisation in terms of SetSetSet-valued functors. We will then justify these constructions by observing that many natural properties and problems for schematic systems can be expressed in terms of representability.

They begin by going through some of the examples I just listed. Many of these gadgets can be described as functors f:C→Setf: \textsf{C} \to \textsf{Set}f:C→Set for various finite or at least finitely generated categories C\mathsf{C}C. In this business S\textsf{S}S is called a schema and fff is called an instance of that schema.

For example they explain the schema for a simple kind of stock-flow diagram, borrowed from here:

An instance of this schema is called a stock-flow diagram.

Any stock-flow diagram has a set of 'flows', a set of 'stocks', a set of 'links', and a set of 'inflows'. Every flow goes from a stock to a stock, while an inflow comes in from nowhere (as it were) and goes to a stock, and there are links going from stocks to flows (which say which stocks affect which flows).

This example is nice to see, because it's on my mind: @Nathaniel Osgood and I have just developed an approach to stock-flow diagrams that's more in line with how practitioners actually use them. But that's irrelevant here: the above picture is just an example of a schema, or more precisely a quiver that presents a schema.

They also describe a schema for Moore machines with a fixed set AAA of actions and a fixed set OOO of observations. The interesting thing about this schema is that it doesn't explicitly mention states. In trying to understand it, I immediately came up with a different schema, for all Moore machines with a fixed set AAA of actions. This has two objects, state\text{state}state and observation\text{observation}observation, an arrow from state\text{state}state to observation\text{observation}observation, and one arrow from state\text{state}state to state\text{state}state for each action in AAA.

They soon turn to examples of how "natural properties and problems for schematic systems can be expressed in terms of representability". For example, there's a famous schema whose instances are graphs (= quivers). There's a graph KKK with 4 vertices, each with edges going to all 3 other vertices. In the category of graphs, hom(G,K)\text{hom}(G,K)hom(G,K) is the set of 4-colorings of the graph GGG. So, we say KKK represents 4-colorings.

Dually, suppose EEE is the walking edge: the graph with two vertices and one edge from the first vertex to the second. Then hom(E,G)\text{hom}(E, G)hom(E,G) is the set of edges in the graph GGG. We could say EEE corepresents edges. Instead, the thesis talks about 'motifs': in biochemistry, a 'motif' is an interesting small network that can be found inside larger networks. (The walking edge is actually too simple for biochemists to call it a motif, but we can think of it as one.)

The thesis then turns to 'data migration'. Given a functor between schemas, say f ⁣:C→Df \colon \mathsf{C} \to \mathsf{D}f:C→D, there is an obvious way to take any instance of D\mathsf{D}D and turn it into an instance of C\mathsf{C}C. This gives a functor f∗f^\astf∗ from SetD\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{D}}SetD to SetC\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{C}}SetC. This functor has both a left and right adjoint, which in the database community are called Σ\SigmaΣ-migration and Δ\DeltaΔ-migration along fff, respectively. This was discussed extensively in Spivak's book Categories for Scientists.

The thesis more generally uses the term migration for any functor from SetC\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{C}}SetC to SetD\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{D}}SetD. They point out that cocontinuous functors correspond (up to natural isomorphism) to profunctors from C\mathsf{C}C to D\mathsf{D}D. They call these cocontinuous migrations.

They also define 'continuous migrations' in the obvious way.

They give lots of nice examples of cocontinuous and continuous migrations, which I will omit here. :cry:

They define a familial migration to be a functor from SetC\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{C}}SetC to SetD\mathsf{Set}^{\mathsf{D}}SetD that preserves connected limits.

In database-inspired jargon, a migration from SetC\mathsf{Set}^\mathsf{C}SetC to Set\mathsf{Set}Set is called a query, since an object of SetC\mathsf{Set}^\mathsf{C}SetC is an instance of a database, and you might 'query' it in some manner to get a set.

A familial migration from SetC\mathsf{Set}^\mathsf{C}SetC to Set\mathsf{Set}Set is called a duc-query because it's a disjoint unions of conjunctive queries. And clearly, if it looks like a duc and quacks like a duc, it's a duc.

An important example of a familial migration which is neither continuous nor cocontinuous is the migration sending a quiver QQQ to a new quiver Q′Q^′Q′ with the same set of vertices, but whose edges correspond to paths of edges in QQQ.

That is, the free category monad.
